newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn tax plan risks 30 bln DM revenue gap - SPD.
newsitem.headline: Bonn tax plan risks 30 bln DM revenue gap - SPD.

text.p: Bonn's proposed tax reform would cause a revenue shortfall of 30 billion marks ($17.9 billion) in 1999 that would have to be offset by more borrowing or spending cutbacks, a key opposition Social Democrat (SPD) official said on Monday.

The plan, which forecasted a revenue shortfall of about 44 billion marks, badly underestimates the cost of cutting income, corporate and capital gains taxes, Heinz Schleusser, SPD finance minister of North Rhine-Westphalia said in a statement.

"The actual financing gap is clearly higher than 44 billion marks and is not justifiable in the budget," he said. "It is necessary not only to correct the proposed rates, but the basis for proportioning income tax must be systematically adjusted."

Schleusser is the key numbers man on the SPD negotiating team, which met leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government in a rare tax "summit" intended to clear the way for big reforms to boost investment and job creation.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan would lower the top income tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent, something the SPD is reluctant to agree to.
Financing cuts with increased borrowing would endanger Germany's ability to maintain European monetary union stability criteria, Schleusser said.

He said Waigel had underestimated by six billion marks the reduction in revenue due to lower income tax rates, while its calculations on dividend and interest tax cuts was short by another six billion marks, Schleusser said.
The coalition's planned corporate tax cuts would reduce revenues by 25 billion marks in the first few years, not the 10 billion total used in the reform proposal, he said.
The coalition also overestimated the amount of revenue that would be generated by changes in property tax laws, leaving a total financing gap of about 30 billion marks, Schleusser said.
